business_patterns.top_pattern: CO HMO authorized acute admissions surge
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: Commercial Individual inpatient spend in CO HMO acute hospitals with authorized stays
business_patterns.pattern_details: The largest cost signal is a CO HMO acute hospital increase tied to authorized inpatient stays. The increase is overwhelmingly volume-driven, with admissions and claims rising sharply while average paid per admit fell. This points to more inpatient use getting through the system rather than broad acute reimbursement inflation.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: This is the single biggest inpatient cost driver and it will not be solved by rate action alone if admission growth is the core issue.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: UM operations should audit CO HMO inpatient authorization approvals, admission sources, and level-of-care decisions for acute hospital stays, then hand confirmed rate issues to reimbursement policy only where utilization does not explain the increase.
evidence_summary: CO HMO acute hospital authorized stays added about $81.6M.
Admissions increased by 1,994 and claims increased by 1,054.
Average paid per admit fell by about $31.8K, showing the spend increase is not being driven by higher unit cost.
The increase is highly concentrated in a repeated authorized inpatient pattern.

business_patterns.top_pattern: CT PPO authorized inpatient growth in acute hospitals
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: Commercial Individual inpatient spend in CT PPO acute hospitals and long term care hospitals with authorized stays
key_driver_codes: Chemotherapy without Acute Leukemia as Secondary Diagnosis with CC
business_patterns.pattern_details: CT shows a second major authorized inpatient utilization story centered in PPO acute hospitals. The core increase comes from materially higher admissions with only minor change in paid per admit in the main acute segment, while smaller chemotherapy and LTCH components add tail pressure. This is primarily an inpatient volume management issue.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: A large admission-led trend in CT PPO can keep compounding even if unit reimbursement is mostly stable.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: UM operations should review CT PPO authorization rules, admission pathways, and discharge destination patterns, with separate attention to acute medical admissions and downstream LTCH use.
evidence_summary: CT PPO acute hospital authorized stays added about $68.9M, driving a total pattern of about $69.5M.
The main CT acute segment added 1,422 admissions and 737 claims.
Average paid per admit in the main CT acute segment increased by only about $440, so utilization is the dominant lever.
Smaller CT add-ons include chemotherapy-related acute pressure and LTCH utilization.

business_patterns.top_pattern: CA acute hospitals are under both admission and unit-cost pressure
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: Commercial Individual inpatient spend in CA acute hospitals across HMO, EPO, and PPO
key_driver_codes: Chemotherapy without Acute Leukemia as Secondary Diagnosis with CC
Major Hematological and Immunological Diagnoses Except Sickle Cell Crisis and Coagulation Disorders with CC
business_patterns.pattern_details: CA acute hospital spend is rising through a mix of more inpatient activity and higher paid per admit. The largest block is CA HMO acute hospital business, where authorized stays show both higher admissions and materially higher paid per admit, and CA EPO adds another sizable acute utilization increase. Chemotherapy, hematology, back problems, and O'Connor Hospital are recurring contributors inside the broader acute pattern.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: CA is not just seeing more inpatient use; it is also seeing richer or more expensive acute episodes, which requires joint UM and reimbursement action.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Run a combined CA inpatient action plan: UM should review admission and level-of-care appropriateness, while network and reimbursement teams validate contract performance and case-rate behavior for the acute hospital providers and DRGs showing both volume and unit-cost growth.
evidence_summary: The CA acute hospital pattern totals about $45.3M across HMO, EPO, and PPO.
CA HMO acute hospital authorized stays added about $27.7M with 422 more admissions and about $24.7K higher paid per admit.
CA EPO acute hospital utilization added about $12.9M with 264 more admissions even though paid per admit was slightly down in that segment.
Additional CA acute pressure appears at O'Connor Hospital and in chemotherapy, hematology, and back-problem DRGs.

business_patterns.top_pattern: Authorization coding and facility mapping must be fixed before broad action
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: Commercial Individual inpatient interpretation in CA, CO, OH, and WI where authorization coding shifts or facility mapping gaps are material
business_patterns.pattern_details: A material share of the trend is sitting in authorization code movement and unmapped facility buckets, especially in CA and CO. That means part of the observed provider mix, site-of-care, and authorization story may be classification noise rather than true business change. This is a gating validation issue and should be corrected before expanding utilization or contracting actions.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: If the auth flag or facility type is misclassified, the organization can target the wrong providers, the wrong UM rules, or the wrong sites of care.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Data quality and UM operations should reconcile authorization code assignment and facility mapping for CA, CO, OH, and WI, then rerun downstream utilization and provider analyses on the corrected populations.
business_patterns.validation_reason: The source groups explicitly show authorization code distribution shifts and unmapped facility values, which can distort business conclusions until corrected.
evidence_summary: CA authorization code distribution contributed about $7.2M and CO contributed about $7.0M, with another $1.5M in OH and WI.
CA EPO spend in Not Mapped facilities added about $7.5M.
CA HMO spend in Not Mapped facilities added about $4.0M, and CO HMO added about $3.6M.
These signals indicate classification movement that can change how authorization and site-of-care patterns appear.

business_patterns.top_pattern: Specialized facility mix is shifting toward higher-cost settings
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: Commercial Individual inpatient spend in CHILDRENS, LONG TERM CARE HOSPITAL, Physical Rehab, and CRITICAL ACCESS facilities
key_driver_codes: Aftercare, Musculoskeletal System and Connective Tissue with CC
Other Digestive System Diagnoses with MCC
business_patterns.pattern_details: Beyond standard acute hospitals, spend is moving into specialized inpatient settings that carry very high episode cost. The biggest examples are CA and CO Children's hospital HMO business, with LTCH and Physical Rehab adding smaller but recurring pressure across WI, CA, FL, and TX; CO Critical Access also adds an admission-driven tail. This is a site-of-care and referral mix pattern more than a single-product pricing issue.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Specialized facility use can bypass standard acute controls and can materially raise total episode cost through referral and transfer behavior.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Network finance and UM should review referral pathways, transfer criteria, and contract performance for children's hospitals, LTCH, rehab, and critical access facilities, starting with CA and CO where the dollar impact is highest.
evidence_summary: The specialized facility pattern totals about $20.0M.
CA HMO Children's added about $7.0M with only 6 more admissions but about $44.5K higher paid per admit.
CO HMO Children's added about $5.7M with 64 more admissions and about $88.9K higher paid per admit.
WI LTCH and rehab-related patterns, plus CA, FL, and TX Physical Rehab, show repeated smaller increases in high-cost non-acute settings.

business_patterns.top_pattern: Acute inpatient cost pressure is concentrated at a small set of providers
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: Commercial Individual inpatient spend in HMO and POS acute hospitals concentrated at named providers
key_driver_codes: Aftercare, Musculoskeletal System and Connective Tissue with CC
Other Digestive System Diagnoses with MCC
Major Hematological and Immunological Diagnoses Except Sickle Cell Crisis and Coagulation Disorders with CC
business_patterns.pattern_details: A meaningful share of residual inpatient growth is concentrated at a small number of hospitals rather than spread evenly across the book. Medical City Plano, Dearborn County Hospital, and AdventHealth North Pinellas all show material increases tied to more admissions and higher paid per admit, with TX POS adding a separate admission-led layer at Medical City Plano. This is a targeted provider economics issue with clearer contracting and case review levers than a broad market trend.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Concentrated provider pressure is more actionable and financially precise than systemwide benefit or policy changes.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Network finance and reimbursement policy should pull contract and case-mix detail for the named providers, then pair with UM to validate whether the increases reflect rate behavior, case severity, or avoidable admissions.
business_patterns.validation_reason: Several provider spikes are flagged as low baseline or low volume, so case comparability and claim integrity should be confirmed before major contracting action.
evidence_summary: This provider-concentrated pattern totals about $10.1M.
Medical City Plano added about $2.0M in TX HMO acute stays with 46 more admissions and about $43.1K higher paid per admit.
Dearborn County Hospital added about $839K in IN HMO acute stays with 18 more admissions and about $46.6K higher paid per admit.
AdventHealth North Pinellas added about $543K in FL HMO acute stays, and TX POS acute activity at Medical City Plano added another $873K through higher admissions.

business_patterns.top_pattern: Inpatient oncology and chemotherapy complications are a distinct cost trend
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: Commercial Individual inpatient oncology and chemotherapy-related admissions in WI and CA
key_driver_codes: Chemotherapy without Acute Leukemia as Secondary Diagnosis with CC
business_patterns.pattern_details: Oncology is showing up as its own inpatient story rather than just a general medical admission trend. WI has a clear chemotherapy admission increase, while CA also shows chemo-related complications such as pancytopenia and neutropenia driving additional inpatient spend; a smaller WI POS acute chemotherapy signal reinforces the pattern. The action path here is oncology-specific care management, not generic inpatient policy.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Chemotherapy admissions and treatment-related complications usually need different interventions than standard inpatient medical utilization.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Clinical and UM teams should review oncology admission pathways, supportive care management, and opportunities to prevent or redirect chemotherapy-related stays through outpatient oncology protocols.
evidence_summary: The oncology-related pattern totals about $5.6M.
WI chemotherapy admissions added about $3.3M with 90 more admissions and about $12.2K higher paid per admit.
CA chemo-related pancytopenia added about $620K and neutropenia added about $505K.
WI POS acute chemotherapy added another about $688K in operational inpatient pressure.

business_patterns.top_pattern: Rare catastrophic and other low-volume high-cost cases are emerging across multiple states
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: Commercial Individual inpatient spend from rare catastrophic, sepsis, post-surgical, orthopedic aftercare, and other high-cost outlier cases
key_driver_codes: ECMO or Tracheostomy with Mechanical Ventilation >96 Hours or Principal Diagnosis Except Face, Mouth and Neck with Major O.R. Procedures
Septicemia or Severe Sepsis without Mechanical Ventilation >96 Hours with MCC
Infectious and Parasitic Diseases with O.R. Procedures with MCC
Aftercare, Musculoskeletal System and Connective Tissue with CC
Other Digestive System Diagnoses with MCC
Cirrhosis and Alcoholic Hepatitis with MCC
business_patterns.pattern_details: Several states show small-count but very expensive inpatient cases that are large enough to move trend despite limited volume. These include ECMO or tracheostomy-type cases in TX, rare digestive and respiratory cases, sepsis, cirrhosis, orthopedic aftercare, and post-procedure complications across CA, CO, FL, IN, OH, and WI. This is best handled as case-level outlier management and validation, not as a broad utilization policy signal.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: A few catastrophic or unusual cases can materially swing results and require different action than broad provider or authorization changes.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Send these cases to clinical review for case-level validation, catastrophic case management, and coding confirmation before using them to drive broader policy or network decisions.
business_patterns.validation_reason: Most source groups are flagged as low baseline, low volume, or small-n admissions, so case-level confirmation is needed before broad action.
evidence_summary: This outlier pattern totals about $11.2M across multiple states.
TX ECMO or tracheostomy-type cases at Medical City Plano added about $1.4M from only a few admissions, with paid per admit often above $150K and up to about $226K.
A broader multi-state rare-case cluster added about $4.3M, including very high-cost digestive, fracture, respiratory failure, and sepsis cases.
CO orthopedic aftercare added about $1.7M, CA rare clinical cases added about $2.3M, and smaller sepsis, respiratory infection, and cirrhosis outliers appear across CA, FL, IN, OH, and WI.

executive_summary.headline: The core story is concentrated authorized inpatient growth in CO and CT, layered with CA acute cost inflation, specialized site-of-care shifts, and a material auth/facility mapping issue that must be fixed before broader action.
executive_summary.primary_business_message: Most of the actionable spend increase sits in authorized inpatient hospital use, especially CO HMO and CT PPO, with CA adding a large mixed volume and unit-cost acute hospital pattern. At the same time, provider concentration, movement into children's and rehab-type settings, and clear authorization or mapping distortions show that UM, network, reimbursement, and data-quality teams all have a role. Oncology and rare catastrophic cases are meaningful but should be managed through focused clinical pathways rather than broad utilization policy.
recommended_focus_order: Validate authorization code distribution and Not Mapped facility classification in CA, CO, OH, and WI before expanding broad interventions.
Attack CO HMO and CT PPO authorized acute inpatient admission growth through UM review of approvals, admission pathways, and level-of-care decisions.
Run targeted CA acute hospital and specialized facility actions with joint UM, network, and reimbursement review, then escalate named provider contract reviews where pressure is concentrated.

notes: All 40 analytical groups were assigned to one business pattern.
Authorization code shifts and Not Mapped facility buckets were consolidated into a single gating validation pattern.
Children's, LTCH, Physical Rehab, and Critical Access findings were grouped as a specialized site-of-care pattern.
Oncology and chemotherapy-related inpatient findings were kept separate from rare catastrophic and other low-volume clinical outliers.
Segment attribution is weak for 49% of cards (49 of 99) on segment_by [service_area_state]; add those dimensions to the stage's dimension or carry-through list to attribute them at cell level.
Merged 25 immaterial segment group(s) into residual groups labelled with their literal segment values.
